meta.title: Who really said "I have hardly ever known a mathematician who was able to reason"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Stephen Hawking — it is Plato, Republic Book VII, 531e, written around 375 BC. And in the dialogue the line belongs to Glaucon, not Socrates.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I have hardly ever known a mathematician who was able to reason'?
meta.ogDescription: Plato wrote it in the Republic around 375 BC, roughly 2,350 years before Stephen Hawking was born — and he gave the line to Glaucon.

answer.label: Not Stephen Hawking — actually Plato
answer.authorDates: c. 427 – c. 347 BC · Athenian philosopher, founder of the Academy
answer.sourceLine: The line comes from Book VII of Plato’s Republic, at Stephanus page 531e, written around 375 BC. Two further precisions the internet version loses: inside the dialogue the remark is Glaucon’s, not Socrates’, and Benjamin Jowett’s standard English rendering reads “capable of reasoning,” not “able to reason.”
answer.confidenceText: Disputed as to Hawking, who is out by roughly 2,350 years. The Plato attribution itself is solid.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Glaucon, replying to Socrates — not Socrates himself

source.excerpt:
What do you mean? I said; the prelude or what? Do you not know that all this is but the prelude to the actual strain which we have to learn? For you surely would not regard the skilled mathematician as a dialectician?

Assuredly not, he said; I have hardly ever known a mathematician who was capable of reasoning.
trail: Wikiquote’s Stephen Hawking page ↗ lists this sentence in its Misattributed section and reassigns it in one line: “Plato, The Republic, Book VII, 531-E.”

We confirmed that against the primary text rather than taking it on trust. In Benjamin Jowett’s translation on Project Gutenberg ↗, Book VII runs: “For you surely would not regard the skilled mathematician as a dialectician? / Assuredly not, he said; I have hardly ever known a mathematician who was capable of reasoning.”

The “he said” matters. Socrates is the narrator of the Republic, so the line is his interlocutor’s — Glaucon ↗, Plato’s brother. Jowett’s own running analysis of the book confirms it, giving Glaucon the reply “I have hardly ever known a mathematician who could reason.” Attributing the jibe to Socrates is a second, quieter error.

The famous phrasing is Jowett’s, not Plato’s. Jowett himself renders it two ways in one volume (“capable of reasoning” in the dialogue, “could reason” in his analysis), and Paul Shorey’s Loeb translation of 1935 ↗ does not contain the word “mathematician” here at all — we read it, and at 531e it runs “…suppose that experts in these matters are reasoners and dialecticians?” “No, by Zeus,” he said, “except a very few whom I have met.” We found no published translation reading exactly “able to reason”; that wording looks like a loose retelling of Jowett that hardened as it spread.
source.excerptNote: Quoted from Jowett’s translation as published in Project Gutenberg eBook #1497 ↗, which we read directly. Note the wording: Jowett has “capable of reasoning.” The version that circulates under Hawking’s name says “able to reason.”

source.rightsNote: The Greek original is roughly 2,400 years old. The English shown here is Benjamin Jowett’s ↗ translation; Jowett died in 1893 and the translation is nineteenth-century, so it is comfortably in the United States public domain — which is why Project Gutenberg ↗ can publish it in full. Note that later translations are a different matter: Shorey’s Loeb version was first published in 1930–35 and is not equivalently free.

author.bio: Plato was an Athenian philosopher, a student of Socrates and the teacher of Aristotle, and the founder of the Academy. He wrote in dialogue rather than treatise, which is precisely why quoting him is treacherous: the words on the page belong to characters, and the character speaking is often not Socrates and often not endorsed by Plato. The Republic, written around 375 BC, is his longest and most quoted work.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: The line reads like a physicist needling his own field, which is most of why it ended up under Stephen Hawking’s name.

items.why: Hawking was born in 1942. Wikiquote ↗ lists the sentence among his Misattributed quotations and points to Plato’s Republic, Book VII, 531-E — a text older by some 2,350 years.
Even people who correctly trace the line to the Republic tend to give it to Socrates, who narrates the dialogue. In Jowett’s text ↗ the remark is the reply Socrates receives — Glaucon’s, not his.
The circulating sentence is not quite any published translation. Jowett ↗ has “capable of reasoning” in the dialogue and “could reason” in his analysis; we found no edition reading “able to reason.”

misattribution.truthLine: It is Plato’s, it is about 2,350 years older than the man usually credited with it, and in the dialogue it is Glaucon who says it. Read Book VII in full ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The remark is not a joke about mathematicians being stupid. In Book VII Socrates is arguing that arithmetic, geometry and astronomy are only the prelude to the real subject — dialectic, the discipline of giving and taking an account of why something is true. Glaucon agrees a little too eagerly, and the jibe is his way of conceding that technical skill and genuine reasoning come apart.

That is also why it has survived: it is one of the oldest surviving statements of a complaint every technical field still makes about itself. Which makes it unusually easy to mistake for something a modern physicist said last week.
context.pull: Technical skill is the prelude, not the strain.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's Stephen Hawking page lists "I have hardly ever known a mathematician who was able to reason." in its Misattributed section, attributing it to Plato, The Republic, Book VII, 531-E.

Project Gutenberg eBook #1497 is Plato's Republic translated by Benjamin Jowett, and its Book VII dialogue reads "Assuredly not, he said; I have hardly ever known a mathematician who was capable of reasoning." — with Jowett's analysis section giving Glaucon "I have hardly ever known a mathematician who could reason."
Wikipedia dates Plato's Republic to c. 375 BC and describes Glaucon as one of its interlocutors.
Wikiquote gives Plato's dates as c. 427 BC to c. 347 BC.
Benjamin Jowett lived 1817-1893 and translated Plato into English.

Paul Shorey's Loeb translation of The Republic (vol. 2, 1935) renders the 531e exchange as "...suppose that experts in these matters are reasoners and dialecticians?" "No, by Zeus," he said, "except a very few whom I have met." — read directly from the Internet Archive full text, confirming Shorey does not use the "hardly ever known a mathematician" phrasing.
